title: Mass Movements
intro: Mass movements are gravity-driven downslope movements of rock and loose material. Learn how geologists describe and classify them, what weakens a slope, and how creep, slumps, flows and falls differ.

sections.title: What counts as a mass movement

img.alt: Creep, slump, translational movement, and flow are shown moving downslope in different ways.

steps.title: Gravity moves material downslope
bullets: **Mass movement** (mass wasting) is the downslope movement of rock or loose surface material under gravity.
Geologists distinguish types rather than calling every event a landslide. A useful description identifies the material, its speed, how it moves, and how much water it contains.
Events range from extremely slow movement to sudden failures. Avalanches are outside the scope of this unit.

steps.title: Describe the movement, not just the hazard
bullets: Material may move as a coherent block, as loose fragments, or as a water-rich mixture.
The movement style and speed help distinguish a landslide from a flow, creep or fall.
A single slope can experience different kinds of movement as its water content, strength or geometry changes.

boxes.text: A specific name communicates what moved and how. That makes it easier to compare events and recognize the conditions that could produce them.
For any event ask: what material, how fast, what movement style, and how wet?
Mass movement is the broad category. A landslide is not a precise description of every kind of slope movement.

sourceNotes: Instructor's ERTH 209 deck, Mass Movements, slides 3-5; the slide deck excludes avalanches.
OpenGeology, 10 Mass Wasting: https://opengeology.org/textbook/10-mass-wasting/ . Used as a supporting explanation; wording here is original.

sections.title: Why slopes fail

img.alt: Gravity pulls material downhill while water and a weak subsurface layer can reduce slope stability.

steps.title: Driving forces and resistance
bullets: Gravity pulls slope material downhill. A steeper slope increases the part of gravity acting parallel to the slope.
Material strength resists movement. Cohesion and friction help hold grains and blocks in place.
Water can add weight and reduce resistance, while added structures can increase the load on a slope.

steps.title: Weak layers and changing slopes
bullets: A saturated sand or clay layer, weak bedding, joints parallel to the surface, or metamorphic foliation can provide a surface along which material slips.
A weak layer that meets the hillside can allow a block to move downslope.
Weathering breaks down strong rock into weaker surface material. Roots can help hold soil together, so removing vegetation can make a slope less stable.

boxes.text: Failure begins when the downhill forces become greater than the slope's resistance. Water, steepening, added load and weakened material can shift that balance.
Think of a tug-of-war: gravity pulls down the slope; material strength holds it back.
Water does not affect every slope in just one way: it can add weight, lubricate a weak surface, or change how clay behaves.

sourceNotes: Instructor's ERTH 209 deck, Mass Movements, slides 6 and 16-20.
OpenGeology, 10.1-10.2, used to clarify slope forces and triggers; wording here is original.

sections.title: Creep and slumps

img.alt: The diagram contrasts slow creep with a slump that rotates along a curved failure surface.

steps.title: Creep is slow but visible
bullets: **Creep** is the very slow downhill movement of loose surface material.
Repeated wetting and drying or freezing and thawing can nudge grains over time.
Look for tilted trees, poles, walls or foundations: these can reveal gradual movement.

steps.title: A slump moves as blocks
bullets: A **slump** is a rotational landslide in which coherent blocks of loose material move along a curved, spoon-shaped failure surface.
The moving mass can break into smaller blocks as it descends.
Unlike creep, a slump is a distinct slope failure rather than slow grain-by-grain movement.

boxes.text: Creep can be hard to notice on a single day, but small seasonal movements accumulate. A slump leaves a clearer curved scar and displaced blocks.
Creep: slow grains. Slump: coherent blocks on a curved surface.
A slump's curved failure surface is different from the more planar surface often associated with a translational slide.

sourceNotes: Instructor's ERTH 209 deck, Mass Movements, slides 7-9.
OpenGeology, 10.3, used as a supporting explanation; wording here is original.

sections.title: Mudflows, debris flows and lahars

img.alt: A water-rich flow moves sediment downslope, alongside examples of creep, slump, and translational movement.

steps.title: Water-rich flows
bullets: A **mudflow** is a fast-moving mixture dominated by water and fine sediment.
A **debris flow** carries a wider range of material, including gravel and large boulders, within a flowing mixture.
More water and a steeper route can help a flow move faster; less water and a gentler slope tend to slow it.

steps.title: Volcanic flows
bullets: A **lahar** is a volcanic mud or debris flow. Ash and other volcanic sediment mix with water from rain or melted snow and ice.
A lahar can travel down river valleys, so areas far from a volcano's summit may still be exposed.
The material and water content distinguish a lahar from a lava flow.

boxes.text: Water can turn loose sediment into a mobile mixture. Once moving, a flow can carry both fine particles and large rock fragments downhill.
Mudflow: mostly fine sediment. Debris flow: mixed sizes, including boulders. Lahar: volcanic debris mixed with water.
A lahar is not molten lava. It is a water-rich flow of volcanic debris.

sourceNotes: Instructor's ERTH 209 deck, Mass Movements, slides 21-39.
OpenGeology, 10.3, used as a supporting explanation; wording here is original.

sections.title: Landslides and falls

img.alt: A slope diagram distinguishes coherent blocks moving along a surface from material falling from a steep face.

steps.title: Landslides move along a surface
bullets: A **rock landslide** moves mainly solid rock; a **debris landslide** moves mostly loose surface material.
Landslides can move suddenly along a failure surface, so a large event may be extremely dangerous.
The material involved and the style of movement are both part of naming the event.

steps.title: Falls detach from steep slopes
bullets: In a **rockfall**, rock detaches from a steep face and drops, bounces or rolls downslope.
Fragments may collect at the base of a cliff as talus.
A fall is different from a landslide: the material is not travelling as one coherent block along a continuous failure surface.

boxes.text: Naming the moving material helps explain what the deposit contains; naming the movement helps distinguish a falling block from a sliding one.
Landslide: moves along a surface. Fall: detaches from a steep face and drops or bounces.
A rock slide and a debris slide are distinguished by the material; a rockfall is distinguished by its falling motion.

sourceNotes: Instructor's ERTH 209 deck, Mass Movements, slides 40-48.
OpenGeology, 10.3, used as a supporting explanation; wording here is original.

sections.title: Water and weak layers

img.alt: Water enters a slope and a weak layer provides a possible failure surface under gravity.

steps.title: Water changes slope strength
bullets: Water can load a slope, lubricate a weak layer, and change how clay particles interact.
Some clays swell when wet. In quick clay, a change in water and salt conditions can cause a once-firm sediment to lose strength.
Rainfall can trigger failure when a slope is already weakened or a slip surface becomes saturated.

steps.title: Recognize planes of weakness
bullets: Potential weak surfaces include bedding, joints, faults and metamorphic foliation.
If a weak layer slopes toward and reaches an exposed hillside, it can provide a route for slope failure.
A strong-looking surface can conceal a weak layer below it, so the geometry underground matters.

boxes.text: A slope may remain in place until water or another trigger reduces its strength enough for gravity to move the material.
When evaluating water, ask: did it add weight, lubricate a surface, or change the clay?
The presence of water alone does not identify a movement type. Describe the material and how it moves as well.

sourceNotes: Instructor's ERTH 209 deck, Mass Movements, slides 10, 16-20 and 49-56.
OpenGeology, 10.1-10.3, used as a supporting explanation; wording here is original.

sections.title: Submarine landslides

img.alt: Gravity and weak layers can destabilize sediment, including material on an underwater slope.

steps.title: Movement can happen underwater
bullets: Mass movement also occurs beneath the ocean, where sediment can fail and travel downslope along the seafloor.
A submarine landslide can disturb infrastructure on the seabed, including communication cables.
Sediment-rich underwater flows can continue moving after the initial slope failure.

steps.title: The same forces still matter
bullets: Gravity remains the driving force, while slope geometry, sediment strength and pore-water conditions affect stability.
A change in pressure or loading can help trigger failure in underwater sediment.
The resulting movement can travel a long way from its starting point.

boxes.text: The ocean floor is not motionless: a sediment failure can move a large volume of material and affect equipment far from shore.
Underwater does not mean no gravity; seafloor sediment can still fail and flow downslope.
A submarine landslide is still a mass movement, even when the material moves below the water rather than on a dry hillside.

sourceNotes: Instructor's ERTH 209 deck, Mass Movements, slides 57-68.
OpenGeology, 10 Mass Wasting, used as a supporting explanation; wording here is original.

cards.back: Gravity-driven downslope movement of rock or loose surface material.
Very slow downhill movement of loose material, often revealed by tilted trees, poles or walls.
cards.short: Slow movement; look for tilted features.

cards.back: A rotational landslide in which coherent blocks move along a curved failure surface.
cards.short: Blocks move along a curved surface.

cards.back: A water-rich flow dominated by fine sediment.
A flowing mixture that can carry sediment from fine particles to large boulders.
cards.short: A water-rich flow with mixed-size debris.

cards.back: A volcanic mud or debris flow made when water mixes with volcanic sediment.
Rock detaches from a steep slope and drops, bounces or rolls downslope.
cards.short: Detached rock falls from a steep face.

cards.back: A surface such as bedding, a joint or foliation that can guide slope failure.
cards.short: A weak surface that can guide slope failure.

quiz.q: What is the main force that drives mass movement downslope?
quiz.why: Gravity pulls rock and loose material downhill.

quiz.q: Which observation is a common sign of creep?
options: A tilted tree or telephone pole
A new crystal in a geode
quiz.why: Slow seasonal movement can gradually tilt features rooted in the moving material.

quiz.q: What is distinctive about the failure surface of a slump?
quiz.why: Slumps move as coherent blocks along a curved, spoon-shaped surface.

quiz.q: Which movement is a water-rich mixture dominated by fine sediment?
quiz.why: A mudflow is dominated by water and fine sediment.

quiz.q: What material makes a lahar volcanic?
options: Dry sand with no volcanic material
quiz.why: A lahar is a water-rich flow of volcanic ash and other debris.

quiz.q: Which combination can reduce slope stability?
options: A gentler slope and dry material
quiz.why: Steepness increases the downhill force, and water can add weight or weaken a slip surface.

quiz.q: Which is an example of a plane of weakness in rock?
quiz.why: Bedding, joints, faults and foliation can all provide weak surfaces.

quiz.q: How does a rockfall differ from a landslide?
options: Rock detaches and drops or bounces from a steep face
It moves only as a slow creep
quiz.why: A fall is characterized by detached material dropping, bouncing or rolling.
